Where it began

Javed Miandad was born in Karachi on 12 June 1957, one of seven in his family. His parents had come from Palanpur in Gujarat, where his father had helped look after the sports clubs for the Nawab. Cricket ran right through the family: three of his brothers, Anwar, Sohail and Bashir, played first-class cricket, and his nephew Faisal Iqbal went on to play Tests.

Abdul Hafeez Kardar, Pakistan's first Test captain, saw him play in the 1970s and called him the discovery of the decade. Breaking into a batting order that included Zaheer Abbas, Majid Khan and Mushtaq Mohammad was no small thing, but he managed it.

The player

He arrived in style. On his Test debut, against New Zealand at Lahore in October 1976, he made 163, at the time the youngest man to score a hundred in his first Test. Two matches later he made 206 at Karachi, aged 19, and took from George Headley a record for the youngest Test double-century that had stood for 47 years.

He went on to play 124 Tests, making 8,832 runs at 52.57 with 23 hundreds and 43 fifties. His best was 280 not out against India at Hyderabad in the 1982-83 series, during a stand of 451 with Mudassar Nazar that equalled the highest for any wicket in Tests. He was the first batsman to make a hundred in both his first and his hundredth Test, and he made six double-centuries in all. He captained Pakistan in 34 Tests, winning 14 and losing only six, and led them to series wins over England both at home and away.

What made him special

No one batted quite like him. He was unconventional as a batsman and as a captain, with a technique all his own and a control that historians and opponents alike admired. His greatest moment came in Sharjah in 1986, in the final of the Austral-Asia Cup against India. Pakistan needed four off the last ball. He hit Chetan Sharma for six, the first time an international match had been won like that, finished on 116 not out and became a national hero.

His bowling was more of a hobby. Seventeen Test wickets at 40.12 suggest his captains were right to keep him busy with the bat.

Away from the middle

He played in six World Cups, among them the one Pakistan won in 1992, and once made nine one-day fifties in a row. He was a Wisden Cricketer of the Year in 1982, received the Pride of Performance in 1986 and the Sitara-i-Imtiaz in 1992, and joined the ICC Hall of Fame in 2009. Afterwards he coached Pakistan three separate times, starting in 1998, worked as a commentator and told his story in his autobiography, Cutting Edge.

And finally

At Hyderabad, on 280 not out, he may well have been heading for the world record when the declaration came. Pakistan went on to win by an innings and 119 runs, so nobody could say the runs went to waste.
